records.claim: Sheldrake's morphic-resonance hypothesis proposes that present organisms can be influenced by patterns associated with previous similar organisms.
The hypothesis treats memory as potentially distributed through recurring natural patterns rather than confined to material storage in individual organisms.
Morphic resonance is framed as a collective or species-level memory process linking similar organisms across space and time.
The proposed mechanism is presented as a form of formative causation that supplements conventional local causal explanations.
Newly established patterns are proposed to become easier to reproduce when similar systems encounter them later.
The theory predicts that learning by one population should alter the subsequent ease with which comparable populations learn the same pattern.
The hypothesis is applied to biological development, instincts and behavioral regularities rather than only to conscious states.
The proposed influence is not described as ordinary local signal transmission between the systems involved.
Morphic resonance is distinct from ordinary genetic inheritance and ordinary learning mechanisms in the author's framework.
Sheldrake has proposed experimental tests involving repeated learning and behavior across separated groups.
The framework remains a heterodox hypothesis and should not be coded as established biological mechanism.
The corpus can be used to examine implications for memory, self-organization and consciousness, but morphic resonance itself is not thereby demonstrated as a consciousness mechanism.
Comparative analysis should keep the original formative-causation claims separate from later spiritual or transpersonal interpretations.
Bohm develops an account of reality emphasizing an undivided whole rather than treating independently existing parts as fundamental.
The implicate order is presented as a deeper order from which the explicate, apparently separated order can unfold.
Ordinary objects and events are treated as manifestations within an explicate order rather than ultimate isolated substances.
Relations and movement are given conceptual priority over a picture of reality composed solely of static independent entities.
Bohm's rheomode experiments with a language emphasizing process and becoming rather than fixed nouns and substances.
Bohm explicitly connects questions about reality's wholeness with questions about consciousness and thought.
Thought is treated as a process that can generate fragmentation when it mistakes its own abstractions for independent reality.
The analysis implies that human self-description can become part of the fragmentation it is trying to understand.
The framework motivates a conception of unity in which distinctions remain real at one level without being ultimate separations.
The theory extends beyond individual minds toward a general account of physical reality and order.
Bohm's implicate-order framework is a philosophical/physical interpretation and should not be conflated with a confirmed quantum theory of consciousness.
The distinction between implicate and explicate order is conceptually different from the claim that consciousness is simply a hidden physical substance.
The source is useful for coding wholeness, fragmentation, process and observer-related concepts while keeping metaphysical extensions explicitly marked.
The interview corpus presents consciousness as a topic that cannot be cleanly isolated from Bohm's broader account of thought, matter and wholeness.
Bohm treats thought as an active process that participates in the fragmentation or clarification of experience.
Consciousness is discussed within a framework of undivided wholeness rather than as an isolated mental substance.
Mind, matter and environment are discussed as dynamically related rather than absolutely separate domains.
Thought can become aware of its own movement and thereby investigate the assumptions that shape perception.
A recurring problem is the tendency of conceptual thought to divide reality into independently existing pieces.
Reality is treated dynamically, with change and movement emphasized over static ontological categories.
The individual self is discussed within a broader field of relationships rather than as an absolutely isolated entity.
The corpus includes interpretations in which consciousness is not exhausted by a private individual perspective, but such extensions require careful provenance coding.
Questions about consciousness are connected to a general conception of order in nature and the cosmos.
Interview statements must be separated from later editorial interpretations and from stronger metaphysical claims attributed to Bohm by others.
Bohm's process language should not automatically be equated with contemporary predictive-processing or information-theoretic mechanisms.
The corpus is best used comparatively, preserving exact interview provenance before turning broad statements into formal theoretical claims.
Pribram's holonomic brain theory proposes that brain processing can be described using distributed wave-like and spectral transformations.
Information relevant to perception and memory is treated as distributed across neural fields rather than stored only in one local site.
Fourier-like transformations provide a mathematical framework for translating between spatial-temporal and spectral descriptions of neural activity.
The theory uses local field potentials, wavelets and related signal representations to model fine-fibered neural processing.
Perception is modeled as an active process in which sensory and cognitive operations address distributed features.
Holonomic accounts emphasize sensory-motor reciprocity in imaging and object perception.
The holographic analogy is used to explain how memory can be represented in distributed neural activity.
Distributed representations offer a candidate mechanism for preserving global patterns without requiring a single central storage location.
A change of representational basis can transform the description of neural information without eliminating the underlying information.
The theory aims to connect measurable neural dynamics to cognitive functions through identifiable transformations.
Holonomic theory is broader than the claim that the brain literally functions as an optical hologram.
The theory is relevant to consciousness research through perception, memory and distributed processing, but does not by itself establish a complete phenomenology.
Claims about quantum or holographic consciousness must be kept separate from the empirically grounded signal-processing components of Pribram's work.
Laszlo proposes an information-bearing field as a fundamental connective layer underlying physical and living systems.
The Akashic-field concept is presented as a way of explaining persistence and transmission of information across systems.
The framework emphasizes interconnectedness of organisms, physical processes and consciousness.
The proposal extends from local biological events to a cosmological picture of a unified information field.
The field is described as conserving information in a manner analogous to a cosmic memory.
Some claimed effects are framed as correlations not adequately explained by ordinary local transmission.
Consciousness is included as part of the broad field-level account of reality proposed by Laszlo.
The source extends its framework to claimed anomalous information transfer involving animals.
The theory links evolutionary development with accumulation and reuse of information patterns.
The Akashic-field account is a heterodox synthesis and should not be treated as a settled physical theory.
The proposed field is conceptually broader than the experimentally established zero-point field of quantum field theory.
Its scientific status depends on whether alleged field effects can be operationalized into reproducible measurements.
Corpus analysis should separate descriptions of established physics from Laszlo's speculative interpretation of those results.
The corpus links questions about God, the universe and consciousness within one explanatory or metaphysical frame.
Consciousness is treated as relevant to the interpretation of cosmological reality rather than only as a local brain phenomenon.
The framing permits interpretations in which consciousness extends beyond individual human perspective, subject to source verification.
The source family addresses questions about ultimate reality rather than restricting analysis to operational neuroscience.
God, universe and consciousness are treated as conceptually related domains rather than independent topics.
A unifying metaphysical interpretation is a central motif of the corpus entry.
The relation between individual consciousness and a larger reality is an implied problem for the corpus.
Questions of consciousness are connected with broader questions of purpose, existence or meaning.
The framework invites claims about consciousness at cosmic or universal scale.
The corpus is explicitly classified as heterodox/extended and its metaphysical claims must not be promoted to scientific findings.
Any empirical support claimed by the source must be separated from philosophical or theological inference during later verification.
A metaphysical identification of consciousness with cosmic reality is distinct from empirical claims about neural mechanisms.
This entry should remain title-level and provenance-pending until the exact source, edition and transmission path are recovered.
Goswami presents consciousness rather than matter as the fundamental basis of reality in his quantum-idealism framework.
Quantum theory is interpreted as compatible with a worldview in which consciousness is ontologically primary.
The role of observation is used to motivate a consciousness-centered interpretation of quantum measurement.
The framework associates conscious observation with the selection of particular measurement outcomes.
Quantum nonlocality is used to support a picture in which separateness is not fundamental at the deepest level.
The source connects quantum physics with a unitary conception of consciousness and reality.
Individual minds are interpreted within a larger consciousness-centered ontology.
The framework allows consciousness to exceed the boundaries of individual biological organisms.
Physical reality is treated as dependent on or emergent within a deeper conscious ground.
The interpretation is heterodox and its quantum-physics claims must be distinguished from standard operational formulations of quantum mechanics.
Using quantum measurement language to motivate idealism is philosophically different from an experimentally demonstrated consciousness-causes-collapse mechanism.
The corpus is useful for comparing observer, unity and idealist claims while preserving a strict distinction between interpretation and established physics.
Changes in conscious perspective or state are presented within a broader model in which consciousness participates in the unfolding of experienced reality.
Hagelin characterizes a unified field as dynamically self-interacting and self-referring, and identifies self-referral with consciousness.
The framework identifies the unified field of fundamental physics with a field of intelligence.
Consciousness is proposed as a fundamental property of the unified level of nature in Hagelin's interpretation.
The diversity of physical phenomena is described as emerging from an underlying unified field.
The proposed mechanism for self-awareness is recursive interaction of a field with itself.
Human consciousness is placed within a universal field rather than treated as an isolated local occurrence.
Hagelin links the proposed unified-field account to training of the human nervous system and meditative access.
The framework explicitly supports a transpersonal conception in which individual consciousness can access a universal consciousness.
The source attempts to ground its metaphysical consciousness claims in mathematical physics and unified-field concepts.
Self-interaction in a physical field is not by itself equivalent to phenomenological self-awareness under standard scientific definitions.
The consciousness interpretation is a heterodox extension and should be coded as attributed proposal rather than consensus physics.
To become empirically discriminating, the self-referral proposal would require measurable signatures that differ from ordinary field dynamics.
Exact source provenance should distinguish Hagelin's physics claims, later institutional presentation and broader consciousness interpretations.
Analytic idealism treats mind or consciousness as fundamental and physical reality as appearing within consciousness rather than producing consciousness.
Kastrup argues that mainstream physicalism faces conceptual problems in treating consciousness as a derivative property of matter.
The framework posits a transpersonal or universal consciousness underlying individual streams of experience.
Individual minds are modeled as dissociated processes or perspectives within a broader conscious field.
The individual self is interpreted as a localized or dissociated perspective rather than an ultimately separate conscious substance.
The experienced physical world is modeled as the representation or appearance of a deeper mental reality.
The framework addresses the problem of how individual subjects can arise without requiring many fundamentally separate consciousnesses.
Brain activity is treated as correlated with experience while the correlation is interpreted through an idealist ontology rather than production by matter alone.
Analytic idealism is explicitly a metaphysical theory of the nature of reality, not a narrow neural mechanism.
Kastrup presents empirical and neuroscientific observations as constraints or support for his metaphysical interpretation.
The theory differs from bottom-up panpsychism by treating one underlying consciousness and dissociation, rather than many micro-conscious units, as fundamental.
The corpus should distinguish Kastrup's arguments from claims that analytic idealism has become scientific consensus.
Changes in dissociation or perspective are used within the framework to explain changes in individual experience.
Kastrup argues that materialism is not the only coherent metaphysical framework for explaining mind and reality.
The book treats consciousness as more fundamental than an emergent byproduct of matter.
The proposed alternative is a non-materialist idealism in which reality is fundamentally mental.
Kastrup presents his idealist case as compatible with, and motivated by, empirical observations rather than as a purely spiritual doctrine.
Individual minds are treated as perspectives within a larger mental reality rather than separate ontological substances.
The physical world is interpreted as the appearance of processes in consciousness rather than a mind-independent material substrate.
The argument challenges materialist assumptions concerning whether consciousness necessarily ends when the individual organism dies.
The dissociation idea is used to explain how apparently separate individual subjects can exist within one underlying consciousness.
The critique targets materialism as an ontology and should not be confused with rejection of empirical neuroscience or physical causal descriptions.
The project is explicitly metaphysical, seeking a coherent ontology rather than a single laboratory mechanism of consciousness.
The proposed worldview has implications for how individuals understand life, identity and the status of personal existence.
Claims presented as philosophical arguments should remain separated from stronger claims that empirical evidence has established idealism.
For comparative coding, the book is valuable as a coherent idealist counterpoint to materialism while requiring strict separation of argument and evidence.
